utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. This is Wednesday, July 11, 2007, and I would like to welcome everyone here. I welcome the witness, the Prosecution, the counsel for Defence and the accused. The cross-examination is now about to start. And 4D is going to start. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon to you. Witness, my name is Vesna Alaburic. I am a lawyer from Zagreb and in this case, together with Nicholas Stewart of the British Bar, who's not here today, I am Defence counsel for General Petkovic. I should like to start off our discussion by clarifying some of your answers to the questions you were asked yesterday. And to do that, let me remind you of the first document shown you by the Prosecutor, which was a three-page note about the plan of arrest of all Muslim males from a settlement up at the front line. The document was dated the 28th of May 1993. Tell me, please, do you remember that document or do we have to produce it and take a look at it together? ?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I prefer the last one.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. It is in the Prosecution binder, and it is 2550, document 2550. P 02550.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I apologise for the interruption. I actually thought that counsel was going to refer to Exhibit 3181, which was the exhibit that related to -- well, I thought she was going to refer to P 3181 but while I'm on my feet let me just say this now. This was the exhibit from yesterday that, about which there was disagreement as to the translation and I can inform everyone in the room that since last night, we resubmitted it to the translation unit and obtained a revised final translation. I don't know that the revision will shed any light on some of the interpretation issues that were raised yesterday but I know that the one change has been made in respect of the word "Muslim" and "balija", and that revised corrected translation now has been distributed to everyone in the room so you all have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't want to deal with the document Mr. Stringer has just mentioned. The document I would like to look at is P 02550 and I can see that there is an error in my question. It is not a three-page document as was recorded on page 1, line 24, but a document that has six lines. And I think -- hope the witness has found the document in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you now, Mr. Van der Grinten, do you know that that alleged plan was ever realised and that in May 1993, all Muslim males were arrested in the settlements up at the front line in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I explained yesterday, this was a message from team M3. So it came from the southern region and to answer your question, that is for me negative. I don't know if it happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the second explanation that I'd like to hear: If we remind ourselves of what you said yesterday about the vehicle, your missions vehicle, which in passing from West to East Mostar was hit and that you assumed that it was hit from a location which was under HVO control. Now in that connection I would like to ask you the following: Did it ever happen that members of the BH army used vehicles of your mission to hide behind the vehicle and cross over from the west to the east bank? Did that ever happen? From the east to the west bank?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. We were confronted with such a situation several times.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, did you ever caution the BH army and said that that kind of behaviour was unacceptable and that they were placing your vehicles in jeopardy by doing that?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did. We complained at the headquarters that they should prevent these kind of situations.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And my third question, the third question I'd like to clear up, it refers to patients and you told us, and it was yesterday -- in yesterday's transcript, pages 61 and 62, you said that patients in the hospital on the east bank, you won't have the transcript but it is the transcript of your testimony yesterday, you don't have to look for it, what you said was that the patients were not ready to go to the hospital on the west bank because of the general fear that something would happen to them on the west bank, and now I would like to ask you in that connection whether the HVO expressed its readiness to take in and treat all the wounded persons and everybody else from the east bank of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was only a proposal, but we were never confronted with, let's say, actions in that direction. So it was only a discussion.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Can we agree, then, that the proposal and that the readiness on the part of the HVO was recorded in your reports, for example the report that we looked at yesterday that was shown to us by the Prosecutor and it was P2789, dated the 15th of June, your report of the 15th of June, can you just confirm whether you did indicate this readiness on the part of the HVO in your reports? If you can tell me, relying on your memory because that is certainly what it says in your report.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can we go to the document, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. The document is 2782 -- no, I apologise, I misspoke, 2782.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: And you are referring to which part of the text?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Point 3, the end of the first section where it says that the medical service of the HVO once again offered to take care of all the wounded, both Muslims and Croats, including people from the east side. Can we then agree that you, in your reports, recorded this readiness on the parts of the HVO to treat all persons needing treatment from East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct but I need to clarify that it was a proposal.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It was a proposal. Now, let's take a look together and see whether the proposal was adopted and if not why not. Tell me, now, the fact that wounded persons and people living in East Mostar, to be treated in the hospital in West Mostar, would that have had a positive impact, positive publicity in the media, for example, both among the international and local public? Would a gesture on the part of the HVO be welcome?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that that is correct, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, tell me, do you know of a single act on the part of the BH army which would allow something to happen which could lead to the HVO being given positive publicity in the national or international media, a single event that you can quote?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we transported by my knowledge, when I recall it correct, three times medicines from the west to the east, and that, of course, was with approval of the HVO management in the west -- in the west bank hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Apart from that, apart from the medicine situation, do you know of anything else which the HVO offered to do which would lead to positive publicity for the HVO which the BH army agreed to? I'm asking you that because in some of the documents that or one of the documents that we saw in this courtroom, it was noted that the BH army did not allow people to go to the west bank to undergo treatment because that would have had a positive impact, positive publicity for the HVO, or rather negative for the BH army. So that's why I'm asking you in that context whether that could be correct.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge. I know that the only thing what came from the east bank was that they knew -- they needed secured transport talking about this. They were afraid that when UNPROFOR was not involved in this, that bringing the wounded people through the confrontation line was not such a good idea.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: There was no obstacle for UNPROFOR to take part in the realisation of this HVO proposal. I assume that UNPROFOR did not reject the possibility of cooperating in transporting people who were wounded to the west bank?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it never came that far.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, the fourth point that I'd like to seek clarification about relates to your testimony about the difficult living conditions of the population in East Mostar at the time that you were there. Tell me, please, to the best of your knowledge, was there some sort of control over movement in East Mostar, the comings and goings, who was going in and leaving East Mostar or could you go there freely whenever you wanted to, that everybody could come and go whenever they wanted to on all sides, I'm talking about control from the aspects of the BH army and the Muslim authorities.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on the east side there were, as there were on the west side, control, check-points, control points, also by the BH army, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did you have any knowledge to the effect that the population of East Mostar had to seek permission if they wished to leave Mostar to go to any other place like Jablanica, for instance?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In the memoirs of Muslim commanders, it was recorded among other things that a large portion of the population in East Mostar wanted to leave East Mostar but that the BH army prevented them from doing so and that in doing so, they used force against the population. Do you have any knowledge about that?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, Witness, you talked to us about the Heliodrom and your visit to Heliodrom, to that prison, and if I understood you correctly, it was a visit in June 1993. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember exactly the date, but I think it was in June, yeah, but it's in one of the reports we saw yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes. Now, since Heliodrom in June 1993 was not -- is not the subject of our indictment, what I want to ask you is this: To your knowledge, the number of prisoners --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, before you pursue I'd like to come back to the previous question that you asked, that we see at line 8 of page 7. You speak of a document or memoirs of Muslim commanders according to which the Muslim population in East Mostar could not -- Mr. Registrar, there seems to be some translation problem. The registrar now says it's okay. All right. Great. So, Ms. Alaburic, in the previous question to the witness that you see on lines 8 of page 7, you state that there were documents of Muslim commanders stating that the Muslims in East Mostar could not leave East Mostar and, as the case may be, force would be used against the Muslim population, and the witness answered, "No, I have no knowledge of that." When you asked the question, on what document were you basing your question?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question was based on memoirs in particular Mr. Esad Sejtanic's book and I was referring to a passage which, pursuant to the latest ruling of this Trial Chamber in relation to the exhibits that were admitted with Witness Pellnas, I'm not sure if he was a protected witness or not, it was refused by a majority vote of the Trial Chamber, so it was for that reason that I did not introduce the same exhibit. But I thought that I could rely upon memoirs and books. I can back that up with books and even documents which are in e-court but which have not been okayed as exhibits. Now, during my cross-examination, we can look up the number of the document and we can, of course, put it on e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. You may pursue, move on to the next question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: We were discussing Heliodrom in June, and, witness, I mentioned that in -- the Heliodrom in June is not a subject of the indictment. All I wanted to do was to explain that everything that you said about Heliodrom referred exclusively to June 1993; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. I have to see my reports to answer this in a positive way because I don't remember exactly the date you are mentioning now. So when you show me the number, then I can verify if the date is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about your statement to -- and testimony to the Prosecutor, not a separate document. I don't have to ask about the date of the document because each document is dated. But never mind, if you don't remember, witness, we can move on. I would like us to take a look at the report about a crime, the document written in writing on the 24th of June 1993, given to you. In the document, on that piece of paper, it was recorded that a husband and wife were burnt in a house that had been mined. It was 2835, document 2835.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have a document 2835, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I'll just check whether that number is correct. I'm being -- I'm told that it is 2935, the right number, 2935. Thank you for that. And I apologise, witness, for giving you the wrong number. The right number is 2935.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now let's look at 2941, please. 2941, the last passage, Mr. Stringer read out that sentence too, but we didn't dwell on it and I'd like to stay with the sentence today. So in the last portion, in the first sentence there, you mention that -- you caution about the various crimes committed by the HVO and then you specify burning people in their own homes and in the very next sentence, you say, "We cannot confirm any of the crimes." Now my question is: Would it be right to conclude that you cannot confirm that what is stated in this handwritten document actually happened? Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We were of course not witnessing this crime. The only thing what we could confirm were the names on the papers placed on the trees, as discussed yesterday. By the way, in this report, it says, not confirmed, means that in principle, when we don't mention that specifically, then we had other sources of confirmation.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes. But your sentence is, "We cannot confirm any of the cases." That's what your sentence says, you cannot confirm from any source.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here mentioned not all but you are referring to the previous document, and only thing what I'm saying is after receiving that document we went to the spot as explained yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. You explained that. I'm just trying to show from this other document that your sentence: [In English] "We cannot confirm any case," [Interpretation] refers also to the information mentioned in the previous sentence about burning people in their houses. But may we agree on this?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is your question?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: My question is whether this sentence, "We cannot confirm any case," refers to burning people in their houses and does this refer to the burning of the two persons mentioned in the previous document? Or does it refer to other incidents of burning in other houses?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, to enlighten the witness, maybe you should read the end of the sentence to him because after "cannot confirm any case," there is a comma and then there is a sentence after this which you're not mentioning.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the witness has the document before him. He can see it. And he has probably read these sentences more than once now so I believe he can answer the question. He said that some other things refer to pieces of paper hanging on trees, so that is not in dispute.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Madam, once again, the principle how we wrote the report is when it were rumours, we mentioned that it were rumours. When it were rumours not confirmed by any possibility by us, then you see that in the text. And that is the same here, I think. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Well, that's precisely what I wanted us to confirm, that this statement that no cases can be confirmed also refers to the other document. We can now move on.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I would like to stick with this document for a moment. It is striking that we have a handwritten document in English and a handwritten document in B/C/S. I seem to understand that they were fixed on trees. Did you yourself see them fixed on a tree or on different trees and taken down?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These are not the papers from the trees, by the way, Your Honour. That's a misunderstanding. But when we went to the spot, we saw papers on the street and that was checked by our interpreter, as I explained yesterday, because she translated the text on the papers on the tree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: So one of these two and I suppose it's the one in English is a translation written by your translator?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: And how did you get possession of the B/C/S language text? Was it given to you or was it picked up from the street?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was given to us. The Croatian text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: By whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't recall the name who gave it, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] I would like to ask Their Honours, in order to avoid wasting time now that we are dealing with these documents, one can see that these two documents are written on the same kind of paper, from the same pad. So it seems that somebody who provided the document in B/C/S also gave the whole pad and this could be translated later on. You can see the date, it's been torn from the same pad, both what the translator wrote and what some person gave to this person. But this is illogical, it's contradictory so could this be clarified?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, General Praljak has a very -- scrutinises everything, makes note of the following. I noticed the same thing but I wanted counsel to do the cross-examination but the B/C/S text is written in B/C/S and the first sentence, first words are, "Help me" in English but it's torn from an agenda because we have, you know, hours, like 6.00, 6.30 and so on. That's in B/C/S and it seems your interpreter translated in English what was written in B/C/S and it starts with, "Please" et cetera. So this is the question put to you by General Praljak, rightly so. Why is it that you are handed a text in B/C/S and at the same time the text is translated on a piece of paper that comes exactly from the same agenda or pad? Does it mean that the person who handed you the text in B/C/S had the pad and gave the pad over to the interpreter who immediately translated what was written? Could you tell us exactly what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That last was the situation. So it was -- it was-- it is the agenda paper of our interpreter, that's correct. So she put the text on the agenda and made, on our request, the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: But how did the B/C/S text get on paper of your agenda?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was not my agenda.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It looks exactly the same. Of course, it is possible that it is not yours but it is a bit striking that it seems to be identical. Were they very widespread? Did everyone have a block like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't recall. I don't recall it but it definitely is in different handwriting, as you can see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I couldn't help noticing. Did you bring this pads from the Netherlands or did you buy it in Mostar or somewhere else in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was her notice book, it's not mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Ah, it's hers, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mine was smaller without the timings in the left so...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there could have been another situation where you and the interpreter could see those pieces of paper on trees and then maybe your interpreter could transcribe in B/C/S what is written on those sheets of paper that are on the trees. And but this is something that cannot work because the handwriting in English is different from the handwriting in B/C/S. So there is a mystery here, we need Sherlock Holmes to solve it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Unfortunately, Your Honour, I can't solve this mystery at this moment after 14 years. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the dates do not correspond either. In the B/C/S text, it says June, and in the English text, it says July, I think. June, sorry, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Well, there is a mystery, and we all note this. Ms. Alaburic, you may resume.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, yesterday listening to your testimony concerning the 30th of June 1993, and the events which ensued after this important date, I had the impression that it is your opinion that a relatively minor attack by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was launched on the HVO and that this was followed by large-scale detentions of Muslim men of military age. First of all, I wish to ask you the following: Would I be correct in concluding that you described the 30th of June as an attack by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina on the HVO in response to a question by my learned friend Mr. Stringer? Is that what happened on that day?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: As part of this attack, did something happen which might be considered unusual in an army, something that would make it not just an ordinary attack by one army against another army but something else? Do you have any knowledge of this?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you are talking about. I don't understand what the question is, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In that attack, did Muslims who were soldiers of the HVO play any special role?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was not there. I was not at the spot. I didn't see the operation so I can't answer this question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And you have no knowledge as to what happened on the 30th of June and whether the Muslims who were in the HVO played an important role such as, for example, treason against the army they had been part of until that moment?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I stick to that what -- what is in our report. According to --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Well, sir, let's look at your report, then. Look at document 3025 in the Prosecutor's bundle. 3025. A report by your mission for the 30th of June, and look at 5, the fifth paragraph. In that paragraph, it says the following: "This morning between 3 and 4.00, Muslim soldiers in the HVO battalion which was in the area of Bijelo Polje north of Mostar attacked their own Croatian troops and positions in the area, the village of Rastani on the west bank, and the Northern Barracks. These attacks were coordinated in advance and had the support of the 1st Mostar Brigade. The commander of that Brigade Midhad Hujdur was killed in action. Thirty wounded were brought to the HVO hospital, 30 wounded soldiers, two wounded civilians and three dead bodies of HVO soldiers. The doctor stated that there were many more soldiers killed." Witness, did you ever hear before now that what happened on the 30th of June was in fact treason by the Muslims in the HVO and the loss of positions by the HVO precisely because of the treason of their own soldiers of Muslim ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, this was the explanation of the operation by the HVO doctor in the west bank hospital and we were -- what we did is we noticed his story and that is what you find here. And probably he was very well informed, so ...

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, was it like this or not, to the best of your knowledge? You were a European monitor?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That has nothing to do with my mission, Madam, but let me clarify it again. We went to the west bank hospital and this was the story we heard. We were not at the spot. I didn't observe the operation.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, can you tell me, then, what you actually do know? How do you know that on the 30th of June there was actually an attack by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina on the HVO? How do you know about this?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because it was told to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Who told you that?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, that is in the report. The report says, "After visiting we got the next HVO statement by the military doctor in charge." For me it's crystal clear that it came from that doctor. So... I don't got the point, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. In your reports, you report partly what you are told by your collocutors, we agree on that, don't you? And you don't go into it further, investigating whether it's true or not. You just report what you are told and what you consider to be relevant; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, and that means that we try to verify this later on, of course, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Did you attempt to verify what happened on the 30th of June?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was very difficult to verify it because access to Mostar was denied from that moment. So this is actually the only statement we had on that particular day. And then, freedom of movement was refused by HVO, so we didn't had actually that many opportunities to confirm this.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And up to the end of your stay there, until the end of August, you received no information and you never checked what actually happened on the 30th of June. Is that what you want to tell us?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were very willing to check it but there was no access to the officials since then, that moment, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes. We will look at your other reports, and we will verify this. Now, in this same document, you express some assessments. You say that this attack by the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina was the first step in connecting or linking up the Jablanica area with the Mostar area. That's in the last paragraph of this document. You can see that, Witness. To the best of your knowledge, after this action on the 30th of June, that is in July 1993, was communication between Mostar and Jablanica in fact established, and did the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina gain control over the area north of Mostar on the left bank of the Neretva?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. This is an assessment so ...

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. I assume you had regular meetings with your colleagues from UNPROFOR and you were informed of what they had observed and what their conclusions were; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We discussed this probably several times with the Spanish Battalion, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What did they tell you about this event?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You don't remember?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's impossible to recall it when it is not in one of my reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How much time do I have left? Because I'll have to leave out some questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You had one hour altogether, so, registrar, could you tell us how much time is left?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 35 minutes?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And you've used so far 32 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have three minutes left?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Ms. Alaburic, you were granted one hour, one full hour, if I'm right. Let me check.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're right, you had 35 minutes so altogether you had 35 minutes you already used 32 minutes and you have three minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Three minutes. Your Honours, some Defence teams will not be using all the time allotted to them and there is an agreement among us that I will use only my time, but if my colleague, Ms. Nozica doesn't use up all the time left to the other Defence teams, I will make use of the time that's left over.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, in my bundle of documents, document number P 03952, 3952, that's a document issued by the European monitors on the 6th of August 1993, human rights situation, and I'll draw your attention to one sentence only. Point 2(B), second paragraph. In the first paragraph, because it's not my intention to appear to be skipping over things, it says some five weeks ago the HVO decided on a large-scale operation to arrest all able-bodied Muslims from 16 to -- in order to -- and so on. "This operation followed a rebellion by the Muslim soldiers in the HVO who gave an opportunity to the army of BH to open a corridor for horse transport between Jablanica and Mostar along the River Neretva." So this is dated August 1993. Tell us, Witness, do you have any knowledge or did your monitors gain any information, to establish that it's correct that on the 30th of June, there was a rebellion of the Muslims who rebelled against their own army, the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That remark of the doctor in the west hospital was a story we heard later on, at various times. So it was not the first time. We heard that later on more.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, unfortunately, I have to stop now because I've run out of time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you. I hope I will have an opportunity to continue. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Now for Mr. Coric, please. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours, good afternoon to everybody. Good afternoon, sir. I see the document is distributing our documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, in the course of my examination, I'll make use of the documents you have received now but also the ones you have before you from the Prosecutor. I would first like to go back to a topic you were asked about yesterday by His Honour Judge Antonetti, the Presiding Judge, so first -- and I think you've answered this question, but it doesn't do any harm to go over it again -- Mr. Nissen was your superior from the time you arrived in Herzegovina until about the end of July; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nissen and you, like all the other members of your mission, teams M1 and M2, had the same interpreter; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's not correct.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: (redacted) Oh, yes, you already said that you don't know that. When you arrived in the mission, the interpreter we talked about yesterday and whom I'm asking you about today was he already employed or were you there when he or she was in the process of getting this job?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you talking about the interpreter of M2, of our team? You mean the female, our female interpreter? No, she was not a member of the pool. As I told yesterday we were able to select her ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, in response to a question from the Bench, when you were shown part of your statement, in which you say that you intentionally employed a Muslim interpreter because you were afraid that a Croat could inform their Croat leaders, you said in response to that question that the Croats who were employed in Siroki Brijeg, you didn't use in Mostar precisely for that reason. You also said, in response, that the most important reason for which you had employed that particular Muslim interpreter, lady Muslim interpreter, was that she had studied English and that it was also a point in her favour that she lived in Mostar in a handy place because it was easier for you to pick her up. Now, I assume that the Croats knew English too, the ones that you employed in Siroki Brijeg, otherwise they wouldn't have been employed by you in the first place; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Now, I'm not quite clear on this. Why weren't you afraid that a Muslim interpreter could inform his or her own leaders, just as you were afraid that the Croats might inform their leaders, especially when the person lived in Mostar and I'm sure she had a lot of acquaintances, and it's -- among Muslim leaders, that she knew them too because she lived there. So why weren't you afraid of that?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course, Madam, you never know in such a situation but, as I said, we were able to select her ourselves. The other ones were already -- sorry, the other ones in Siroki Brijeg were already in the pool and doing that work for some time. So by making our own selection, we were in favourite position to select someone we trust.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: You told us that you already testified before this Tribunal in the Naletilic trial and I read the transcript because we were produced it by the Prosecutor. You said that you weren't afraid that that person could convoy information to the Muslim side because she lived on the west bank. That's what you said, and it was recorded on page 7428 of the transcript. Do you remember that that was one of the arguments you put forward for your selection?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that it is in the transcript, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me: You don't speak or understand the language spoken by the domicile population in Mostar, do you? That is to say whether we call it Croatian or Croatian-Serbian, Serbo-Croatian, I don't mind at this point in time but what I'm asking you is you don't speak it or understand it, do you?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's correct. Then only some courtesy words.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: When you went to meetings on the east bank, negotiations, you took the lady interpreter with you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: And when you arrived on the spot, the interpreter, I assume, talked to the people on the east bank or at least she interpreted. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: I conclude that, since you yourself don't know the language, you couldn't actually know what she was saying in her mother tongue; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: I think that hypothetically speaking, the interpreter could have, in view of the fact that you didn't understand anything, she could have said whatever she wanted to and translated something quite different to you, or kept silent, kept quiet about something that she might have heard. That is possible, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is always possible, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, also in response to a question in the Naletilic Martinovic trial, you said you found the interpreter yourself and asked whether they would work for you. Now technically speaking I'm interested in knowing how you came across her or rather this person in the street. Did you ask her, do you want to interpret for us? Or did you receive a recommendation? How did you come to employ her? How did you come into contact with this individual in the first place?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't recall exactly how we met her.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, did you run any checks on her, take down her particulars and then checked out her CV by services who had better resources for that kind of thing because as far as I understood you yesterday, you didn't have any intelligence service to do this for you?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. So that was only done by ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, I'd like to round off this topic by this final question: Had that person perhaps worked for one of the warring parties, you would have no way of knowing, of learning, whether that was the case, because you didn't have that intelligence to check it out, unless you happened to notice something by your own observations or, if you happened to hear about something like that, you would have no other means of checking, right?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Ms. Tomasegovic Tomic, I'm just wondering, is this -- are you fishing in the dark or is there any foundation for all these questions you are putting? Do you have the slightest point of attachment for these suspicions that you utter? MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it was very difficult for me to check out the information because the name of the lady interpreter has been kept secret, confidential, and the previous witness was asked not to mention her name for her own safety but I'm asking these questions because that person is quite obviously the most important source of this person's information. So if it is firsthand information, and he is secondhand information when it comes to information, then as Defence counsel, I have to check out her credibility and perhaps bring into doubt her authenticity and the authenticity of her statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, I apologise for this intervention but I'm -- I've been informed that a revision or redaction to the record is going to be -- need to be made before the 30 minutes passes. Something was said a few minutes ago and if -- I apologise for this but if we could briefly go into private session I could explain it in one minute to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Yes, well, the Trial Chamber would ask the lawyer to be quite sure that we are not losing any time. By these questions, are you trying perhaps to establish whether the witness received information from the interpreter that could have misled him? Is that what you are trying to prove? MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] I'll come to that part when I come to specific events in my cross-examination, events that the interpreter informed them about. This was an introduction, and it was Your Honour's questions that prompted me, Your Honour's questions yesterday, to go through this introductory part, so that when I get to specific events, such as the events in Mostar and Ilici, then I'll go back to the question of the interpreter and who she was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [No interpretation] MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor yesterday showed you a diagram, a schematic, compiled by the UN dated the 22nd of July 1993. It is document P10025. You have it in the Prosecution binder. It's the thick binder in front of you, sir, not the thin one. And we can have it on e-court. The first page after the title page, and the title there is, "The Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, political personages." And yesterday when you looked at the document you said that you agreed with the schematic and that it corresponded to the information that you had yourself. I'd like us now to take a look at this page together and we'll concentrate on the right side, and it says here, under political personalities that within the HZ HB, there was the Ministry of Police, led by the minister, and then subordinate to him was the chief of police, and underneath the police chief was the chief of military police, Valentin Coric. Do you see that, going down the right side of the diagram?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: What I've just read out, in view of the fact that you said that that corresponded to your information as well, this would correspond to the information you had and how you understood the situation; is that correct? Because you told us yesterday that you agreed with that diagram.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't say that. I said yesterday that it was a piece of information we got from the Spanish Battalion intel section, and it gave us a possibility to go into the structure and verify also our own information.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: I'll find that portion of your testimony. Just give me a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Just for the record, Mr. President, the witness was not asked about this page at all during his direct examination. He was directed to a different page and that's the only other page he was asked to comment upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm not sure I understand what the objection is. Is Mr. Stringer saying that we cannot go into pages of documents that he introduces unless he's directly looked -- referred to those pages? I just want a clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. He was not -- it was not an objection on his part. He simply said that when he asked questions, they were not addressed to that page but to another page. That's all. It was not an objection. But Defence counsel is entitled to address another page, naturally. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor asked you the following question and it was recorded on page 80, line 23 of yesterday's transcript. He asks you: Was this document -- did you have access to this document? Did you have the document at the time that you were in Mostar? And your answer was on page 81, lines 2 and 3, "Yes, it existed at the time." And that's why I said that it coincided with that date, the 22nd. Now, from this it was logical to me that it was information which you did not challenge and which you considered to be authentic. So if you used the document and if it helped you in your work, as you say, then that would be the case. If I have made the wrong conclusion I apologise, but that seemed logical to me.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that you made the wrong conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: So that means that you consider that the information in this document, which was placed by the United Nations at your disposal, that they were incorrect?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm sorry, Madam, that's not what I am saying. I only said it was information we used, as we used various sources, to verify our own information.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: But if you had your own information, then you could compare your information with the information contained here. Did you have any information of your own at all? And did you, in fact, compare them to the information contained in this document? And once you had compared the two, if you did, did you agree, did they coincide, did they agree, or did you have no position in the matter?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Depends on the information we needed to verify, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you haven't answered my question. I put a clear question. You have a document in front of you, the document is a UN document, and you say that they are one of your sources of information. Apart from that, that means you had your own information and other information. Now, if you compare all those different, all that different information, and based on your experience there and the knowledge you had, does this document correspond to the truth or not or do you not know? Yes, no, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was a good document what showed the structure of HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me now, please, you said you had information to the effect that Mr. Berko Pusic was the deputy of the military police -- deputy military police chief; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is this a question?

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was the way he was introduced to us, yeah, as the deputy of Mr. Coric.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, did you know that until the end of June 1993, in the structure of the military police of the HZ HB, the post of deputy chief of the military police did not in fact exist? There was only the post of assistant military police chief. Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I only know what I just told you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Would you now take a look at the documents in that thin binder of ours? It says, 5D documents. I'd like to show you two documents after which I'll ask my question. So on e-court, please, may we have the following documents? P 02963 is the first one. It's the first document that you have in that binder in front of you. Everybody has the document in the courtroom and in the translation booths. It is a proposal for appointment of officers to the military police administration dated the 26th of June 1993. Mr. Coric signed the document. We mentioned him several times. And in the introductory part of the document it says, "I hereby propose," and then point 1, "that Mr. Radoslav Lavric be relieved of his duties as assistant chief of the military police administration and appointed as deputy chief of the military police administration. We'll now look at the second document and then I'll ask you my questions after we've seen that one as well. So document number 2 now, please, which is a document dated the 28th of June 1993. It is a decision which says that in the administration -- military police administration, the document number is P 02985, it is a decision where it says that, as deputy chief of the military police, Mr. Radoslav Lavric is appointed. So Mr. Radoslav Lavric is appointed deputy head of the military police, in the military police administration. Now, sir, in these documents we see that the deputy head, previously the assistant, was somebody else, not Mr. Berko Pusic. You've never seen these documents before; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: You mean you haven't seen them or no, that is not right? Which?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never saw them.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Now that you have seen these documents, do you allow for the possibility that Mr. Berko Pusic or, rather, that his post that you were told that his post was different, the name of the post he occupied was different to what it was?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. At that moment maybe. But I repeat, he was introduced as the deputy of Mr. Coric in the HVO MOD building to our team and we spoke to him several times. That were our own observations and the most important ones for the team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, you said he was introduced to you as the deputy of Mr. Coric but who introduced him to you? Was it Mr. Coric or the floor sweeper? Who told you that Mr. Pusic was the deputy of Mr. Coric?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm very sorry, sir, that I can't answer this question because I don't remember. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: I would just like to point out that this is a Prosecution binder, and we can see in the translation that in the original B/C/S it says 28, 06, which means the 28th of June, as the date of the document, and the English text, the wrong date is mentioned. It's the 28th of August. Just to clear that up so we don't have to go back to that question later on. I've just noticed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: That's right, Mr. President, I was going to point that out. The translation, the English translation, has an incorrect date. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, sir, you said that on the 16th of June 1993, you met with Mr. Coric and Mr. Pusic in one of the offices -- in someone's office, you don't know whose office it was, but tell me who attended that meeting, who was there in addition to yourself on -- from your mission, who else was there?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my team member, Mr. Amatriain, so we were four.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, was the meeting scheduled previously? I mean earlier on. Was it scheduled in advance?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Normally, we ask for a meeting, yeah, so it was probably scheduled. I mean, we normally made an appointment to meet the gentlemen.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not interested in what the situation was normally like but whether you remember that specific meeting. Was it scheduled in advance? If you don't remember, it doesn't matter because many years have gone by since then.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true, but we had a lot of questions after the visit of the Heliodrom, so it was an important -- it was from great importance to have answers on these questions as soon as possible, so I suppose that we arranged that as soon as possible. It was an arranged meeting, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, do you happen to remember whether Mr. Coric spoke English?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, did you have an interpreter? Do you remember that? Did you take an interpreter to the meeting with you?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember, but that was always -- the interpreter in fact was always a member of the team and there for translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Coric perhaps have an interpreter of his own at the meeting? Do you happen to remember? Or did he use your interpreter, or did he perhaps speak English? You say you don't remember but any way --

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: May we now have a look at a document that was shown to you yesterday by the Prosecutor? It is the document describing the meeting, your report, P 02806 is the document number. It's your own report dated the 16th of June 1993, and we have point 3 where it says, "Meetings," and if we look at the document carefully, underneath the heading which is, meetings, the first thing is says is the following sentence: "We introduced ourselves." Have you found it, sir?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: P 02806 is the document number, and the Prosecutor showed it to you yesterday. It is your own report of the 16th of June. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: You have it on your screen. And look at point 3, meeting, meetings, and it says, "We introduced ourselves for the first time to Mr. Valentin Coric, chief of the HVO military police." Then there is a gap and it says, "We met," and it says who, and who you talked to. You can see it. I don't have to read it out for you. We discussed, et cetera, now what I'm interested in is why where it says, Mr. Coric, and if you meant with him and Mr. Berko Pusic together why it doesn't say we met Mr. Coric and Mr. Berko Pusic and discussed such and such. But with Mr. Coric, it just says we introduced ourselves for the first time to Mr. Valentin Coric, it doesn't say what you discussed, nor does it say that he was present during your meeting with Mr. Pusic. So why does it say it that way if you talked to both these two men together? I think that if the topics of discussion were that important and you say they were, then Mr. Coric, in your view, was the superior to Mr. Pusic, you should have written it in a different way, if both these men attended the meeting and you discussed the same issues together with them.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It's now time to take a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, yesterday you described your visit to Heliodrom. Tell me, were you assisted by the same interpreter, lady interpreter, we mentioned today when you visited Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, you told us that at Heliodrom, you spoke with the warden and in the document showed to you by the Prosecutor, we can all take a look at it, it's P 02721, under point 3, entitled, "Meetings and persons spoken to," it says that you spoke to the deputy warden, and in the statement you gave to the investigators of the OTP you also said that you spoke to the deputy. So can you tell me which is correct? Did you speak to the warden or the deputy warden, as this report suggests?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When there is an inconsistency in this matter, then I can't recall who of the two it was, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, sir, do you remember the name of this person?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: I assume you didn't note down the name because if you had, it would possibly be included in your report, had you known it when you were compiling the report, am I right?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Normally we do.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, you told us in your report that only HVO soldiers had mattresses, whereas all others slept on the floor. In this document you have before you, which I've opened, under point 6, entitled, "Assessment," first passage, last sentence, it says, "Only HVO soldiers and women have beds to sleep in. Everybody else has only mattresses on the floor." And you said the same in your statement. What is in your report is the same thing you said to the investigators. But what is correct? What it says here or what you told us yesterday?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is in the statement probably is correct. I have to clarify that because the statements -- the interviews that were made also with the help of my personal notes. I didn't have them here. So the interviews now were without that so --

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I understand. We don't have to go into it further. But yesterday you said that when you visited Heliodrom, you used the word that you went to the barracks. What does the word "barracks" mean to you? Sometimes it's interpreted as soldiers' quarters, barracks. So what building does that suggest to you?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe it was not the right expression but it was a fixed infrastructure with buildings.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Were these traditional-type buildings? How many buildings did you visit? Or were they buildings intended for some purpose, such as schools, gyms and so on? Can you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the only thing what I can recall that it were normal buildings, but some parts were reconstructed and we visited also the cells. There were also cells we visited.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: How many prisoners did you speak to? And was your interpreter the one who mediated or did they speak English?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly the number of prisoners, and I will explain the procedure. In the team, our interpreter only was involved when she was asked to translate. So in the case that the people we asked were able to speak English, she was not involved. When people -- and that is in general the way we worked. When people didn't were able to speak, for instance, in English, or another language we understood, French or German as well, then she was involved in, as interpreter or translator.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: That's quite clear, and it's quite logical. I was only interested in whether you remembered whether those persons spoke English that you talked to or whether she interpreted. I understand the principle, of course there is no need for interpreting if both sides in a conversation speak the same language.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't recall how many times the people were able to respond in English or the times that she was translating, after 14 years. Maybe you understand that that is hard to remember now.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: I understand, but I do have to put the question. Now, tell me this: You know that the prisoners -- or you said that the prisoners told you they didn't know why they were there and what they had been accused of. I would like us to be quite precise. Did they only tell you that they didn't know why they were there or did they tell you that no indictment had been issued against them or did they perhaps tell you that no criminal report, no charges, had been brought, or did they tell you that they didn't know whether they were under investigation? So do you recall which of these possibilities they mentioned, or don't you remember?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I remember very well that all these questions were answered negative.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, sir, do you know the difference between a criminal report or charges and an indictment?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not a specialist but with common sense I think that I can make the difference.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, then, what the difference is, according to common sense?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that an indictment is based on a completed investigation.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: And a criminal report?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That could be a part or that could be being used for that indictment, for instance.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Who submits a criminal report or who brings charges, and who issues an indictment? Did you know what the law on criminal procedure was that was in force at the time in the area?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who submits a request for an investigation, who issues a decision on an investigation, and who issues a decision on remand, on detention on remand? Do you know what the case was according to the valid legislation in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me: Do you know how long an investigation can take, even in peacetime, let alone in wartime, and what that might depend on? And how long it might take?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I said, I'm not a specialist. So I have to disappoint you because I don't want to speculate.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: I have a number of questions I wanted to put, but I won't waste time on this now, regarding detention and so on. But tell me: When you spoke to those people, did you take their personal details, their first and last names, their dates of birth?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, unfortunately not.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: So when you arrived at that meeting to speak with people about the situation in Heliodrom, you were unable to show them a list of persons, nor ask about particular persons, and ask why each one of them was there? You could only put a general question why are these people here, am I right?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. That was our intention.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please: Mr. Nissen, when he testified here, and this is on page 20508, lines 23 to 25, it's not in these documents here, I'm saying this for the record, for Their Honours and for my learned friend, and on pages 20509, lines 1 to 6, he said that you had instructions from your team in Zagreb not to deal with prisons because that was for the ICRC to deal with, and that for this reason, when you heard or saw something, you would report this to the International Committee of the Red Cross. You said that you purposely did not attempt to enter those premises because that was not your job, not your task, so is it possible that your superiors thought that you, unlike the International Committee of the Red Cross, had neither the necessary expert knowledge nor the training required to deal with these matters and that it was precisely for this reason that that was the job of the ICRC, and not your job? When I say your job, I'm not referring to you personally but to members of your mission in general.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the visit -- to plan a visit to the Heliodrom was of course discussed within the coordination centre. So there was a reason for us to go there. But I'm very familiar that the Red Cross --

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: But tell me -- no. I only want to know whether you know about this standpoint, do you agree with what Mr. Nissen said or is this the first time you've heard this? That's all I want to know. Did you know about this position and would you agree with it in principle, regardless of Heliodrom now, but in general, as a rule, where prisons are concerned?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: To answer your question, the first part, this is the first time that I heard about that statement of Mr. Nissen but I'm of course, as officer, aware of what you told -- just told us about the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: I would now like you to look at document P 02824 in the Prosecutor's bundle, and while we are looking for it, I'll begin my question. As it says in your document which we mentioned previously, the prisoners told you that the food in Heliodrom was not good. Tell me: Did you check where and how food for the prisoners in Heliodrom was prepared while you were there? Because you had conflicting information about this. The authorised official you spoke to told you one thing and the prisoners told you another. So did you go and check and see where and how food was prepared?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: The document I said we should look at, P 02824, is your report of the 17th of June 1993, and in paragraph 5 there is a description of your visit to the prisoners in the headquarters of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It says here, in the sentence before the last, that the prisoners said that the food was very bad, but the same that the ABiH soldiers have, so that's been added. When it says that the soldiers are receiving the same food as the prisoners, and you know that soldiers need to be fed well, this would mean that the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina treated those prisoners, as far as food is concerned, in the best way they were able to at that point in time. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: For this observation, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know that in Heliodrom also, food for the prisoners was prepared in the kitchen of the brigade quartered at Heliodrom and that they received the same food that the members of the HVO units at Heliodrom received? Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: I would now like to move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute for counsel. You just said that the detainees got the same food as HVO members. Do you have documents proving this? MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] I don't have the documents, but witness Josip Praljak told us this in his testimony. I think it was a response to a question I put and he described in great detail how the food was prepared. That's why I asked this. I assumed that if this was the deputy warden, then the gentleman might have received this information because he met those people at the Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: I would now like to move on to two other topics, two events, that are the most striking in your statement, and you used them to explain your personal conviction about some things, confirming the general thesis about the events in Mostar at the time. So first I would like to deal with the visit to that flat that you photographed when you visited it. Yesterday, you said that it was your interpreter who took you to that flat; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who gave the information, and then we asked her to bring us there, yeah, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, you said that the door was opened by a neighbour. Was the door locked and you couldn't open it? Why was it the neighbour who opened the door? Or did I misunderstand this?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It is correct, and that's what I said. But I don't know why and the door was locked.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Did the Prosecutor tell you who -- or rather, sorry, the neighbour, did the neighbour tell you how he got the keys, who had given him the keys to that flat?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ask him?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably we asked, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: And you don't recall what he answered?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately not.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: To me, it seems important if someone moves somebody out of a flat, then that person probably doesn't hand the keys to the next-door neighbour and ask him to water the plants. If somebody is wanting to move in, they would keep the keys. So it might seem unimportant to you but it's very important to me.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That could be that the next neighbour had a duplicate key by the previous people who lived in the apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, I'm going to object to both the question and the answer. I think both the witness and the counsel are speculating at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This is speculation, counsel, but you may continue. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ask what the name of the family was that had lived in the flat which was now empty? And did you record the name of that family?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall the name of the family.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know how many members that family had and how long they had lived in that flat before they either left it or were expelled or whatever happened?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ask the neighbour whether the family were the owners of the flat or tenants or were they using it on some other basis?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could be that we asked it but I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ask the neighbour what his name was? Did you ask the neighbour for identification? Do you remember the neighbour's name?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: I'd now like to move on to the event at Ilici. If I understood the case correctly, a child handed you a message about the event in Ilici. The message said that a Muslim family had been killed and their house burnt down. This was then interpreted to you by your lady interpreter. After that, you went to Ilici, but you did not manage to find that house. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, sir, is it correct that Ilici is a village, a small village, in which all the houses are located along the road used by vehicles, so all the houses are on the right and left-hand side of the road?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: I'll ask a hypothetical question now. If the village of Ilici looks as I describe it, you drive along the road and all the houses line the road on one and the other side, and if you pass through the village from one end to the other, then certainly you would have to come across a gutted house and see it. Would I be correct in saying that?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In such a case, that is possible, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: I have described the village correctly. Unfortunately I don't have a photograph here now, but I will bring one at the first opportunity. You said that you arrived in the village and you saw HVO soldiers fixing some pieces of paper on pillars, posts, trees, am I right?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: You didn't get out of the car, only your interpreter got out of the car. She came to a post, read what it said there, came back to the car and told you what she had seen; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Did she tell you what kind of notice this was? Because it's quite unusual for soldiers to be fixing pieces of paper around, so did she tell you what kind of notice it was?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was an announcement that people with that name were killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Killed or died? Because it's quite odd to see soldiers fixing to trees notices saying that someone had been killed. It's a little unusual.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, but I want to stick to my -- I don't recall. So I have to stick to the report where we wrote what happened. I don't know the number but ...

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: All I saw in the report is what you have told us so far, but what I'd like to know is why didn't you get out of the car yourself and check this? Because if there is a list of names, you don't need an interpreter or a translator. You could at least have checked whether these were the same names that you had been informed about a day or two previously in Mostar. You didn't need an interpreter for that.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is your question?

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Why didn't you get out of the car and check this?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I can't answer.
