utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Your interpreter also told you, and she was your main source of information, later on you said you had some others, that from the 30th of June 1993, until the 5th of July 1993, about 5.000 Muslim men had been arrested and 400 people expelled from their flats or houses, and you explained this in your report. Mr. Nissen, when he testified here, on page 20464, he said that there were rumours or indications about this but nothing tangible. Do you see the difference between what you said and what you told us yesterday and the way in which this information was interpreted by Mr. Nissen? Why did he feel that this was something that was not tangible but you think it's tangible or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm not necessarily objecting to the question. However, since counsel asked -- is asking the witness to comment on the testimony of another person, I think that in fairness, the witness ought to be able to look at his report, the one that's being referred to, in which there is the reference to the 5.000 arrests and 4.000 -- 400 expulsions so the witness can see what he wrote and then compare it to the testimony that's being put to him that is attributed to a different witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Counsel, in order to support your demonstration, first of all it would be a good idea to submit the report to him, then indicate that Mr. Nissen had said such and such and compare that to what he said yesterday. Perhaps you wanted to just gain some time. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm trying to save time. I quoted this precisely as it is in the report, but the Prosecutor can ask this question in redirect. The witness can answer my question as to whether he thought this information was tangible or not. And let's leave Mr. Nissen out of it, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Colonel, could you specify the difference between what Mr. Nissen said and what you yourself can say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the information probably came from our team, so it is the information what was gathered by the team and it was the interpretation of Mr. Nissen during his testimony, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Let's now take a look at another document shown to you yesterday by the Prosecutor, P 03172. You're looking for it, I'll tell you that this is a daily summary for the 4th of July 1993, and in point 4, "Humanitarian activity", there is a description of the situation in the Cap Anamur refugee camp in Capljina. The Prosecutor put some questions to you about this document. He asked you something about the document saying that every night the refugees were threatened by the military police and you responded that that was correct. In the document, under 4, where this incident is described, in sentence 2, it says, "The refugees are under threat almost every night from the military police, which is searching the camp." Do you observe a difference here? It seems to me -- no, you don't? The document, it doesn't say that the military police threatened the refugees. It says that the military police searched the camp. So they were under threat from the search.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, it's not correct. The document says, "These refugees are threatened almost every night by military police searching." So the word "threat" or "threatening" is found in the witness's own report. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] The key word here, and I don't see the difference between what I said and what you just said, I read the document in the Croatian language, the key word is "search," "searching".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: With due respect I don't see why you pretend this, that the original is English, I think and not Croatian, and there is no way that one could identify any word as a key word here. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] I can read it out again in English and then explain why I think that there is an essential difference. I'll need two minutes for that. It says here, "[In English] These refugees are threatened almost every night by MP searching." [Interpretation] If it is a camp in which the refugees are arriving and then, after that, go on to Germany, and that's the logical conclusion, then in a situation if -- where we are dealing with a war, you have the military police, who is able to search the camp, looking for weapons, deserters and so on. That necessarily need not be linked to any threats to individuals, and that kind of search would not do them any harm. So that's why I asked the question. That is the only reason that I asked the question. And my last question is this:

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, yesterday in your statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment. Is it your last, really your last? Because you already used up an hour. Are you going to be given some time by the others or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, we are prepared to give some of our time to whichever counsel wishes to -- needs a little extra time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And how much time out of your time, your very precious time, are you willing to give?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I did wish to retain 15 minutes. However, in light of the gentleman's testimony and what I'm hearing today and what I heard yesterday, it may not be necessary for me to do any cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Then we understand that you are willing to give your time to the Defence of Mr. Coric. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] I just need three more minutes. I just have one more question.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, you told us in your testimony that you had seen HVO forces in the area -- the HV forces in the area you covered. Now, when Mr. Nissen made his statement, and that was recorded on pages 20486 to 20488, and then again on page 20501 and on page 2054 [as interpreted] and 20591, he said that there was frustration because the mission was asked to report on the HV and they didn't see anybody. So they even made jokes and said they would look for the Bosnian navy, which didn't exist, of course. Now, I'm interested in the following. Why did Mr. Nissen not know that you had seen members of the HV or, rather, did you inform Mr. Nissen of having seen members of the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, first, it depends of course, it's very linked to the date of our report where we for the first time were mentioning this, and I can't give you an answer for Mr. Nissen. In principle, our reports were approved, so also read by the head of the coordination centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Your report was from July 1993. That is to say the time when Mr. Nissen was your superior officer. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, counsel. So now let us move on to the next Defence counsel. Mr. Ibrisimovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We probably won't use up all our time and we'll give our time to the Stojic Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I'd like to start off with a few questions about your team, M2. That was the name of your team, wasn't it, the monitoring mission in Mostar, M2, right?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: We have seen a number of reports and you on several occasions mentioned Amigo Jesus, who was your colleague from the team; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Was he with you on the team throughout while were you in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the complete time frame, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Now, that team, Mr. Jesus Amigo, was he the leader of the team or were you the leader of the team, within the M2 team?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it didn't work that way but officially he was deployed earlier so he had the responsibility of summarising the daily reports, and in that respect he was the leader of the team.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: I assume that your colleague from the team had the same information that you had, and that you exchanged information on all the events that you monitored, right, in Mostar and the area in which you were located?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We gathered the information together and discussed it together. We did everything with the team.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: And that's the reason why you signed the reports together, is it?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Having heard that, I assume that you had a very high opinion about your team colleague or a positive opinion of him?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that we were a good team, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Perhaps we will go back to that topic in due course. But now I have a few questions to ask you on behalf of the Pusic Defence or rather the Coric Defence asked some questions about that, that is to say the position and post held by Mr. Pusic. And for me to do that I'd like us to look at a number of documents. I think Their Honours have the documents but I don't know if everybody in the courtroom does. I'd like us to look at the first document, P 02670 shown to you yesterday by the Prosecutor and if you look at the last page of that document, and I think the paragraph number is 5 -- I apologise, the document wasn't shown to you yesterday. I'm going to show you now, and it is paragraph 1 on page 1. And under (a) it says "Herzegovina". Have you found that portion?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you say it again, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: On page 1, we have paragraph 2 and then (a) is Herzegovina and the second point is titled, the situation over all, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then I have it wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, counsel, I think he's looking for an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: 02670 is the number, P 02670.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the wrong document. Yes, I have it here in front of me. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: It's also a monitoring mission report, the 8th of June 1993 is the date. And if we look at paragraph 2(a), we'll come across the name of a major Berislav Pusic, humanitarian commission and Chief of Staff. That's what it says if you look down the paragraph. And underneath that, it says, an HVO delegation. Have you found that?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: I don't want to go into the contents of the document, it deals with an exchange of some kind, but this is a piece of information which the monitoring mission had according to which Mr. Pusic was the Chief of Staff, and that he was a commissioner of the humanitarian commission, and that's what it says in this ECMM document that you have before you.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Now, to go back to another point that Mr. Pusic was introduced to you as the deputy chief of police, so at the same time we have two different pieces of information. One that he was the deputy chief and then from the same establishment we see that he was the Chief of Staff in a document from the same institution. Although to be true, it says, in brackets, TBC. I assume that means to be confirmed?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, and by the way, this comes from the regional centre, Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But it was sent to the teams on the ground in theatre, right, both to Tuzla, Kiseljak and the teams on the ground?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. You can see to who it was sent, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: In response to a question from the Presiding Judge, you couldn't give us much detail as to where you get the information that Mr. Pusic was the deputy chief of police. Perhaps the Prosecutor can help us out because it provided you with certain documents. Well, let's try and clarify the situation. In front of you, you have a document which the number of which is P 9218, it's a diagram or chart of the structure of the military police, and for the record, we received these documents first on the 21st of December 2005, along with another document from the Prosecutor and then we found it on the 65 ter list. But here we see the structure of the military police in the period from October 1992 to July 1993. And there is no mention of Mr. Pusic's name there. We have the chief, the deputy chief, the chiefs of the different departments, but nowhere do we come across Mr. Pusic here. Right?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to this picture, you are right, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: We can turn to another document, P 9232 is the number, which encompasses the period from July 1993 to December 1993. And once again, it's a diagram compiled, I assume, by the Prosecution which was on the witness chart for Tomljanovich, I'm saying that for the record. And once again, Mr. Pusic's name isn't on this diagram. All the major posts are mentioned, all the departments and officers at the head of those departments but nowhere do we come across Mr. Pusic's name, do we?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't find him on this page.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to go back to a document I started off with, the first document that was shown you yesterday by my learned colleague of the Prosecution. P 2496 is the number. Now, if you take a look at point 7, you'll see that it refers to a joint commission and you told us something about that yourself and mention is made of an agreement of some kind to have access to detention centres. 2496 is the document number. Point 7, or section 7.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: The question was about access to prisoners' centres, detention centres, and Mr. Pusic is mentioned and it says that Mr. Pusic does not have authorisation to sign a permit of that kind, and Mr. Pasalic had already signed that, and that's also what it says in the report by the ECMM report. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but this is not an a report from our team. This is signed, as you see, by Mr. Milverton. So we were at that moment not in --

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm not challenging that. I'm not challenging that the man signed the document. But the Prosecution showed you the document yesterday and I know that that was the day you had arrived in Mostar, one -- give or take a day. So that's why I'm showing you the document and the Prosecutor did not focus on this section of the document. We can now go back to what I started off with, and something your colleague, Jesus Amigo, and it seems Mr. Pusic had some contacts and cooperation with him so let's look at that document which is there. For the record it is 6D 00606.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we have the original if anybody would like to take a look at it. I'm at your disposal. Perhaps the witness would like to take a look. There is the signature there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: It says: "To Mr. Berko Pusic, with gratitude for all the assistance, with the deepest gratitude for all the help he gave us in the completion of our tasks. Mostar, October 1992." It seems that Mr. Jesus Amigo, a member of your team, had very good experience with his cooperation with Mr. Pusic.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe I can explain you what is this. Maybe I can explain you what is this. He signs here as HCC, what means head of the coordination centre. This is a courtesy plaque what normally, by that kind of occasions, by saying farewell or whatever was given to the head of the coordination centre. This was probably given by him at the time that he was replacing the head of the coordination centre. This was not given to him as member of the team and not during the time that we were forming M2.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: If you read it carefully, you'll see that your colleague from the M2 team, Jesus Amigo, you can see the English translation, is thanking Mr. Pusic for his cooperation. It is not given to Mr. Jesus, upon his departure from Mostar. That's why I said that he probably had good experience of his cooperation with Mr. Pusic as a member of your team.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. What is the question? I think that's probably right, yeah, that he had a good relationship, but we had as team also a good relationship with Mr. Pusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's take a look at this plaque so that we can look at it, at this plate, so the Judges can see what it is. For the transcript, let me say that this is a plaque, a small plaque, bearing Observation Mission of the European Community, and in red ink on the back, you have the text, which is on 6D 00606. So, Colonel, I have to ask the question: Obviously this is something given by the ECMM.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'd like to explain probably that he gave this replacing the head of the coordination mission because it is signed, just above his signature, you'll find HCC, and so I guess that he did that by replacing the chief of the coordination centre and not as member of the M2 team. And by the way, I don't know at what time this was given, what the date was, because that is quite interesting, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] October.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: October, yeah, that was probably at the moment that he left the mission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: To complete the record it may be allowed to mention that there is a Spanish flag on it along with the European one which shows -- it's also written in Spanish, which shows that it is probably something which is attached to Mr. Jesus, your colleague.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You are fully right, sir, because we didn't had this kind of courtesy plaques within the mission. This comes from the Spanish Battalion and they had this kind of things so probably he got it from the Spanish Battalion to hand it over. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Let's give this back to the counsel, this expression of gratitude back to the counsel, but show it also to the Prosecution, if you please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a brief explanation. It is not a Spanish Battalion document. It says the ECMM, the Spanish flag is at the front because that year Spain presided over the European Union.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's move on to the next counsel, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, good afternoon, Your Honours. I don't believe I will be cross-examining the gentleman because I would be seeking speculative answers in any event, given some of the questions that were raised by the Defence yesterday -- by the Prosecution, that is. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very good. Well, we have two counsels left.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, and I'd like to start off first. And I'd like to say at the outset that my colleague, Peter Murphy, will also be conducting part of the cross-examination once I finish with my own. As far as time is concerned, I'd like to inform the Trial Chamber that the Stojic Defence team has its original one hour allotted to it and we have been given the remaining time left over from the other teams which means that we will certainly continue tomorrow. We won't be able to complete the cross-examination today, and if there is any time left over, Mrs. Alaburic said that she would have some additional questions too which she didn't manage to get through today.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. Just on that before counsel begins I would like to strongly request the Court keep in mind -- the Trial Chamber keep in mind tomorrow because it's a short day for us, allowing or saving enough time for sufficient redirect examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Mr. Stringer, could you tell us how much time you expect for your redirect?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: At the moment, based on the cross-examinations that have so far occurred, I think very -- not very much, maybe 15 minutes or so, subject to the cross-examinations to come.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very good. I will ask the legal officer to do the computation and see where we are in terms of time, so that we are not flooded. You may resume.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I'd just like to say that before I begin my cross-examination, that we are very grateful to the other Defence teams for having given us two hours for cross-examination. However, if we have to curtail that time, or if we don't have time to get through the two hours of cross-examination, we would like to reserve the right to ask that the witness -- or rather to be granted additional time for cross-examination as the witness is in this country and it won't be a technical problem to have him called back, and I believe that the Trial Chamber is clear that this witness, for the most part -- well, I'm going to make my request. He testified about Mr. Stojic throughout most of his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is enough to ask a lot of questions, you know, and I can demonstrate this if you wish. If you're professional I'm sure you'll be able to scan the entire topic in two hours, with this witness. This witness is a follow-up of another witness who already came and already discussed all these topics. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may count on those two hours, I'm convinced that we will manage to complete our cross-examination in time.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Good day, sir. I will be putting questions to you on behalf of the Defence of Mr. Bruno Stojic and my colleague, Mr. Murphy, will continue after I finish. I would now like to focus on that part of your testimony and of your reports that refer to the delivery of medical assistance from the hospital on the west side to the east side. You said that you mediated in the delivery of medical equipment, medicines and so on, on at least three occasions. We have seen your reports from around the 10th of June 1993, referring to requests by the hospital in East Mostar and the goodwill of the hospital in West Mostar to send medicines. I would just like to ask you whether you know that even before the 10th or 11th of June, there were contacts and correspondence between the hospital on the east side and the officials on the west side of Mostar concerning the delivery of medical supplies and medicines to the hospital on the east side.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not by my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Could you please take a look at the pink binder under your left hand right at the bottom, as far as I can see from here? I have provided this to the Prosecutor, the witness. There are three binders for the interpreters. But if the interpreters don't have them, they can get it during the break. Would you look at 2D 00119? You have stickers at the side. Let's take a look at that document. Just tell us when you have found it.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah, I have it here in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: This is a document dated the 3rd of June 1993. Before the period we talked about. And I'll read it. It says, "Referring to information about the shortage of medicines and the sanitary material in the east part of the town under your control, we are willing to offer the required assistance according to your specification immediately and without any conditions. If you are interested in this humanitarian assistance from the central warehouse of the Main Staff of the HZ HB, please hand us your reply through the commission as soon as possible." And this document was signed for the assistant of the head of the Defence department health sector, HZ HB, Brigadier Ivan Bagaric, who sent this letter to the command of the 4th Corps of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Sir, on more than one occasion you said that Mr. Bagaric was the deputy of the director of the hospital in West Mostar. So, please, tell me now whether you know what position he held throughout the time you had contacts with him, that is, that he was the assistant of the head of the Defence department of the sector for health of the HZ HB, in other words, he was the assistant of Mr. Bruno Stojic in charge of health at that time, health care, do you know that?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, please look at document in the same bundle, 2D 00120. It's the next document in the bundle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Ms. Nozica, is that the only question you associate to this document? The witness does not seem to know the document or anything about it. Is that understood?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if you will allow me to go through this series of documents, it will become apparent why I put the documents to the witness and then I will put some questions to the witness about all of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Have you found 2D 00120?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can we conclude from this that this is the response sent by Mr. Arif Pasalic dated the 5th of June 1993, which he is sending to the chief of the headquarters, Chief of Staff, and it says, "Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina" and so on and it says that the RBH army hospital, former institution for hygiene Mostar, "needs supplies and medicines and medical material and therefore we ask you to provide us with the acquisition thereof. Enclosed list of medicines and medical material necessary for the operation of the hospital." Are you aware of this document?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: How did you become familiar with it?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because we handed it over in -- in the western -- the west bank hospital. We transported this message from the east to the west.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Well, you didn't mention it in your reports but I accept your reply. What I'm asking you now is: Is this in fact Mr. Arif Pasalic's reply? Is it logical to conclude that this is his reply to the document we saw previously? It is being sent on the 5th of June, but if you think it's speculation, you needn't answer, although it seems quite self-evident.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I remember, and the effort we took to arrange this, not knowing the first one, signed by Mr. Bagaric, I think that this is the response, yeah, that's correct, because I'm familiar with the list.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. In the Prosecutor's binder, could you please find document P 02703? It's in the Prosecutor's binder, P 02703. And could the usher, if possible, assist the witness and at least remove the documents of those Defence teams that have finished their cross-examination? Because it's a small desk and too many documents. Have you found this document?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: In point 5, in this document, you say the team visited the hospital on the west bank in order to hand a letter from the Commander of the 4th Corps, Arif Pasalic. You say official reply arriving tomorrow, 10th of June 1993, and then you list what is required, what is requested, exchange of teams of doctors, delivery of supplies, and ambulances. You recall this? It's dated the 11th of June 1993.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: In my binder, could you please look at another document, as you have confirmed all this, let's see whether these are documents you remember. It's 2D 00322. It's in the middle of the binder marked by a green sticker. Please tell me when you've found it.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. I have it in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: We have this letter here from Mr. Arif Pasalic. It speaks for itself. But I would only wish to draw attention to point 2, "Please urgently deliver the medicines and medical supplies on the list." If you remember it's that list that we saw just a little while ago enclosed with that letter from Mr. Arif Pasalic dated the 5th of June. Is that the letter from Mr. Arif Pasalic which you carried to the hospital in West Mostar?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it needs a little bit investigation to give that answer because it has to do with the date, the dates of the documents, of course. I mean it was not only one list. We got not only one list. It happened, I think, two or three times. So that's why. It's not that easy for me to say, no, this is exactly what belongs to -- this is the attachment that belongs with this letter. That's difficult for me at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not asking you about the enclosure, let's look at the document itself. Is this a letter from Mr. Arif Pasalic? Is it the letter that you carried that day as you say in your report of the 11th of June 1993? Because you mentioned those three points and explained them so I'm asking you is that the letter?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, then it is the letter.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. Now, please look at your document, P 02721?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, on the previous document, just not have any hesitations, I wonder whether this is the signature of Mr. Pasalic. It looks different from the one we had on other letters and there is something that I cannot read in the original before left of Gospodin Pasalic and that may be signed for or something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it must have been someone who signed on his behalf.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I didn't feel it was very important who signed the document because the witness explained the document and said he received it from the Commander of the 4th Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I assume you found your document P 02721?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You may be able to observe, sir, that I'm following the time sequence and looking at the documents in chronological order. So let's look at the documents accompanying these reports. So the 11th of June 1993. In your report, you say -- let's look at the last sentence, in point 5. It says, "With reference to the letter handed over yesterday to the doctors in the HVO hospital, today, they said that there were no doctors who wanted to change places with those on the east side and that they don't have enough ambulances even for their own needs." You say that you gave the list of medicines to the International Committee of the Red Cross which are needed for the town of Mostar. Let's look at the last sentence in your report where it says, "As for the exchange of specialists between the two hospitals, the HVO on the west side and the Armija on the east side, the doctors on the west side are afraid that they might be badly treated or even arrested if they cross over to the other side. We are trying to negotiate a meeting between the two sides to discuss this situation." You remember this, don't you?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, I'll ask you to look at document 2D 00123. It's somewhere in the middle of the binder.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: This is a letter dated the 11th of June, the same day you compiled your report about the doctors and the ambulances, Defence department, chief of the main medical corps, Colonel Gveric [phoen] and he's referring to a document of the 9th of June, addressed to the main medical headquarters of the HVO. I don't want to take up too much of your time. You may of course take a look. But it says that the delivery of the list of medicines requested is being prepared or the medicines on the list are being prepared. Could you look at the document, please, otherwise you might say it doesn't say that there. As for ambulances I have to tell you that during the aggression on the town of Mostar, 19 vehicles were destroyed and six drivers wounded so the HVO is telling the Muslim side that and say we don't have enough for ourselves and as for specialists, it says that there are no volunteers either among the Muslims or the Croats among the personnel. My colleague, Ms. Alaburic, asked you about this but I'll explain later why I have to put this question. This is the 11th of June and it says that as the conditions of looking after the wounded population and the soldiers are far better here than yours are, we propose for the umpteenth time that you send all your wounded to the HVO war hospital where they will be treated in exactly the same way as our own soldiers according to the Hippocratic Oath and medical ethics. And the HVO main medical staff and I personally guarantee that the treatment will be completely identical. So is this the response by the chief of the main medical staff of the HZ HB which you in fact describe in your report, P 02721, and did you see this letter or were you just told orally that you should convey this message to the persons you spoke to in East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that I saw this message before. The contents, by the way, was well known. The arguments in this letter were well known, so verbally definitely discussed with us, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Evidently, you conveyed these arguments as can be seen in your report of the 11th of June 1993. And then there was more talk of these doctors so I'll put a few more questions about this, but now let's look at a document in the Prosecution bundle, document P 0 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To save time, we know that there was mail that was exchanged with the two hospitals. We know this topic inside out. So if you spend more time on this, it's not going to add anything. So could you please now ask the essential question, essential to you? I mean it's up to you but please ask the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I wish to inform you that all these letters, which are of fundamental importance for the entire Defence, but I don't think I should discuss this before the witness, that I have shown them to witnesses more than once and they were not admitted into evidence because the witnesses knew nothing about them. We have here a witness who knows about these documents, who mentions them, and they are very important. Your Honour stated that in one of your decisions where you said that probably these documents would be admitted through a witness who was familiar with them. So I wish to do that now and this is highly important for the Defence and will not take long. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Could we look at P 02731? P 02731. This is a report of yours of the 12th of June 1993. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Okay. I now wish to draw your attention to point 5 of this report, where you say, "Medicines from the HVO hospital on the west side have been delivered to the Bosnian hospital on the east side, and they will hand over to us the medicines they need urgently." So evidently they needed more medicines. And then in the second part, this is M2 and M3, monitored the departure of four UN helicopters from Medjugorje taking wounded Muslims to Turkey via Split, the Turkish airplanes were waiting in Split. So as of the 12th of June, you submitted a report saying that those medicines had been delivered from the west side to the east side. Can we agree on this?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Definitely.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you tell me what you know about the departure of wounded Muslims? It just says Muslims here, wounded Muslims, via Medjugorje to Turkey via Split, so Medjugorje, Split, Turkey.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall it but it was probably arranged by the UN or the Spanish Battalion, not by ECMM.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I said it says here M2 and M3 monitored the departure from Medjugorje. That's why I'm asking you whether you know about this, because it's in the report of the monitoring mission of the European Community. It says M2 and M3 so I'm just asking you if you know something about this, and if you don't I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. All right. As you say that the medicines were delivered, let's look at 2D 00504.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assume that there will be a break soon. I would like to know exactly when so that I can organise myself. It's the third letter from the bottom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have five more minutes before the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I asked you to look at 2D 00504 in my binder, it's the third document from the end?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I got it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Here we have an order issued by Mr. Gveric to issue medicines as requested by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, a list is enclosed, the quantities should be sufficient for seven days. Please look at document 2D 00321. That's the list. It's found somewhere else, not along with this document, but please look at it, 2D 00321, and tell me whether you can recall you transported these medicines, is this the shipment, can you recall, according to the specification, and if not, all the better, because it would mean that the HVO sent more shipments than you know about, but in any case, can you tell us whether this might be the list of those medicines which you transported on the 11th and then reported in your report of the 12th as having been delivered?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, we delivered at least two times ourselves and one time it was done by the UNPROFOR Spanish platoon, so this is probably one of the lists, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Could we now look at document in the Prosecutor's binder, 2782? I will be referring to point 3 but I just wish to point out what you are able to confirm or what you know. It's your report of the 15th of June 1993. So this is after the incident with the Spanish soldier and you continue to insist and try to organise, as you say at one point, you're the only person in Mostar trying to get the required amounts of medicine and medical supplies to East Mostar and the first place you apply is the hospital in West Mostar, and what you don't get there you try to get through the ICRC and other institutions. You applied to them for things that they cannot give you in the hospital in West Mostar; is that correct? You have to say yes or no for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. Now, please look at point 3 where you go on to say, "In the hospital on the east side, we received a list of urgently needed medicines. We have arranged on the west side for them to get the medicines and tomorrow morning the medical corps of the -- or the medical service of the HVO have promised that they will obtain part of the material." As for oxygen, they will try, if east side provides the empty bottles and pays for it, they have offered again to take care of all the wounded people, Muslims or Croats, including people from the east side. You say, "We asked SpaBat to provide transport of medicines from the west hospital to the east one, but we have been told that they need, before providing the transport, an agreement signed by both parties." Sir, on the 15th of June 1993, when you contacted the doctors on the west side, and in this document you make an error, Mr. Bagaric here is called the director of the hospital -- the deputy of the hospital director, but that was not his post, as we saw from the previous documents, he is the assistant of the head of the health care department of the HZ HB, so you are trying yet again to assist the hospital in East Mostar and the hospital in West Mostar is continuing to offer help and offering to treat people from the east side. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the text, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think it is time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we resume, judges are working hard during the break and they probably solved the mystery of the document. I will give the floor to my fellow judge and he will explain what happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I do not claim any unmerited applause. An interpreter actually has - and I didn't take down her name, I must confess - has drawn my attention to the witness's statement which we have all read and I had even marked. On pages 15 and 16, one finds the explanation for this mysterious document. The fact, as the witness tells it, is that they found this paper with a B/C/S text on it, and later the interpreter wrote down the English version on the back of the same document. So it's recto verso. That explains why the paper looks the same. And can you confirm this, Mr. Van der Grinten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it sounds -- I don't remember it, sir, but it sounds logical -- it's a logical explanation, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Just for the record, Your Honour, the witness's previous testimony was that it came from a notebook that belonged to the interpreter. Just so that's clear on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I was intending to raise this in redirect examination to show the exhibit to the witness but since it's been raised now I think I'll just say this now because during the break we, like the other exhibit, we sent someone into the vault to see if they could find the original exhibit itself and that's what I have here and I will show it to the witness in his redirect examination, just so that it can be made part of the record in that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I join in the discussion? I think I've understood what document this is about, although I didn't listen to the -- I wasn't listening to the interpretation. I don't think it concerns what it says on page 2 of that same document, because if we look at the hours in the left-hand column we will be able to see that that cannot be the case. It is not the reverse side of the same piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if we have time, we'll see this during redirect. So I think Sherlock Holmes worked hard and will continue working. Ms. Nozica, you can resume, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I consider this to be a very important question but I'll carry on and say, by way of introduction, something that this witness knows about, the delivery of medicines and the HVO offer to assist. I'll be winding up this topic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Could you look at document P 02923 next, please? It's in the Prosecutor's binder. P 02923.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: This is your report of the 24th of June 1993. I would like to focus on point 5 and the Prosecutor touched upon that too. Paragraph 2 of point 5 says that you talked to Mr. Bagaric and this is your conversation with him, that's for the transcript, to make it clear, and he refers to the proposal for the exchange of doctors, and in the third sentence, he gives an alternative proposal that the old Mostar hospital be opened up on the west bank - and you say near the battle front, that's your comment - which would serve as a war hospital for everyone, Muslims, Croats, Serbs, members of the HVO and the BH army alike, civilians, et cetera. Now, first of all, let me ask you this: Did you consider that the idea of opening up this hospital was realistic or not?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not realistic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And would you tell me why?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because of the location. And also because the difficulty to secure it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Sir, what does because of the location mean? What do you mean by that? We are going to ask other witnesses that too.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Near the front line.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So is it your assessment that the old hospital building, if you know the one I mean, was closer or further from the front line than the hospital on the east bank of Mostar? You know where the front line was. Now if you know where the old hospital was located, can you say whether it was at roughly the same distance, if not even further from the front line, than the hospital in East Mostar that you visited regularly?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's hard to say because then I need to see the map again, the sketch.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't exactly recall now where it was. What I know that it was very close to the confrontation line, the place he mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, in order to make this clear, was the building in West Mostar?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I have to say in the area held by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, you say that this part was dangerous because of its proximity to the front line. That's your conclusion. So in a way, you refused this proposal because you thought it was unrealistic for those reasons; would that be right?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't -- we didn't refuse anything. It was his proposal.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: But as far as I can see from your reports, you didn't discuss the proposal further with representatives on the east bank or with the authorities, other authorities, both on the east and west banks?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we did but we found out that it was impossible to realise.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. I won't dwell on this, although it is a fairly important question, but Mr. Bagaric, as we can see from this sentence, is making a proposal and he says that in such an unsafe situation that reigned in the hospital, the HVO soldiers and Croats were being treated there too, right along with the Muslims and members of the BH army. That's what would follow from what we see here?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah but I suppose that is not a guarantee that that is not a dangerous place.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well, I didn't ask you that either. Now, it goes on to say in the proposal that in the hospital doctors would work together who were Muslims and Croats, members of the international organisations would supervise treatment, and UNPROFOR would provide security for the hospital. Now, Mr. Bagaric finally proposed meeting, to meet the highest level of the BH army in charge of health affairs, not those from the 4th Corps, to discuss the situation under the presidents of the ECMM. Now do you remember whether this meeting ever came about? Did it ever take place?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It never happened, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did you try to organise a meeting of that kind?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure. We tried to -- we have made an inventory, if it was feasible, yes or not, but we came very quick to the conclusion that it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All I asked you was whether you tried, because I didn't find anything about that in your reports. But take a look at the next document and it is your report of the same date, the 24th of June, but it was written just a few hours later, it is P 02929. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let's look at point 1. We see here that you're trying to discuss the idea that you had, which was in part supported by the HVO, according to which the doctors should cross over from the west bank to the hospital on the east bank, and then you say that team M2 privately contacted some specialists and found out that the specialist physicians on the west bank were mostly Muslims, 70 per cent, and then you say Muslims and Croats are willing to go to the east bank to help their colleagues and exchange them, but only under the following conditions, and there are three conditions which quite obviously weren't met because it didn't go through, but it says here, "Mr. Bruno Stojic, in principle, agreed to our proposal." Am I right in saying that? Is that what it says?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, for the record I'd like to say the following. In the Croatian translation of this document and we received it from the Prosecutor it says that Mr. Bruno Stojic, the chief of the HVO medical corps, whereas in the original, it says, Bruno Stojic, in brackets, HVO and MOD, the Ministry of Defence. So the translation is wrong. I'm saying that for the record.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, sir, take a look at another document relating to the medical corps. It is 2D 00455, and we'll round that off with that document. It is the fourth document from the bottom in my binder. And we see here once again the assistant for the Defence department, the health sector, Ivan Bagaric, on the 16th of September 1993, sends a request to UNPROFOR, to SpaBat, and he once again stresses the former proposal to help the Muslim side to take in civilians, women and children especially, in the Mostar war Croatian hospital as well as other HVO hospitals, "and that we guarantee -- issue guarantees for the treatment of the same as we do for our own. We propose that the control of our work be done by the ICRC, the EC monitors and UNPROFOR and we are doing this for only one reason, a humanitarian reason. We therefore kindly ask you not to attach any political connotations to this matter." Now I know that on the 16th of September you yourself were not in Mostar but I wish to ask you, and we see from this document that the request by the assistant chief of the medical departments, et cetera, is continuing. Did you know that Mr. Bagaric, regardless of the posts you thought he held, he insisted on requests of this kind and attempts of this kind to try and help the sick and wounded, whether they be civilians or members of the BH army on the east bank? So did you know of his efforts and endeavours? You had quite a few contacts with him so did you know he was doing his best to achieve that?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know that because it was -- because we came with request and we set it up more or less.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You didn't know that he was in the HVO structure and the Defence department and that he was the assistant of the head or rather assistant to Mr. Stojic, you didn't know that at that time, am I right in thinking that?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that needs some clarification because we were dealing with this subject with several officials, suddenly he showed up with a white coat and a uniform and a weapon under the white coat, and he at that time, when we met him for the first time, showed that he was in charge of the hospital on the west bank. That is my statement. That was the situation. And we didn't know that he had another function because I never saw the letter you showed me before.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Sir, so you suddenly drew the conclusion that he was the person who controlled the hospital. Would it be right to conclude that before you reached that conclusion, the hospital showed a maximum level of cooperation in its endeavours to help and supply the hospital on the east bank with anything it needed, is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It's not right. Because that was not my conclusion. He presented him as being in charge, so -- and we were the only ones who had access to him and not to anyone else so we had no choice to consider that he was in charge at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: That's not what I asked you, sir. I didn't ask you that at all. You seem to deal with personalities too much. I'm asking you about what happened, events on the ground, but I will ask you about personalities as well. I'm not avoiding that. What I'm asking you is as of the 11th of June, based on the reports that we have seen so far, did you have full cooperation in the hospital on the west bank with respect to delivery of medical equipment and medicines, according to the available capacities of that hospital? That would emerge from your reports but I'd like to ask you now to tell me whether that was so.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had cooperation and they provided us with the things that were asked for. Not full but we had a good cooperation.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not going to ask you whether this is unusual but do you consider it to be important, significant, the two armies were at war, one army was helping the wounded civilians and soldiers of the other army, which it was in conflict with. Now, I'll ask you as a layman would that be considerable an honourable gesture?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Tell me, please, when you gave your statement, what was your assessment of Mr. Bagaric, that is to say that man who was at the head of the hospital, as you concluded, and the contacts on the basis of the contacts you had with him, I don't know what those contacts were but you concluded that he had control of them. Did you think he was a hawk or dove or a hardliner or somebody with a softer approach? What was your opinion?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had the opinion that he was a military man.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did you consider him to be a nationalist and let me remind you, and anybody else who wants to look at page 24 of your statement, you said that he was a nationalist. I'm just reminding you. We don't have to waste time looking it up but just say yes, I did say that; no, I didn't; I don't remember, but that is indeed what you said of him and it's on page 24.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I have one question to ask you about your assessments. Did you see Mr. Bruno Stojic ever in uniform?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Sir, I have to ask you this and you can answer any way you like. Let's leave Mr. Stojic to one side for the moment, although Mr. Bagaric and this department was under him with respect to this assistance in the sense of structure in the Defence department but let's leave him to one side. Now, Mr. Bagaric who did what he did, if you -- your assessment of him was that he was a nationalist, tell me, did you say that on the basis of people's characters, how they were dressed, how they talked to you, on the basis of how nervous they are or not, or did you make that assessment on some more serious indicators? I'm talking about your evaluations. I'm not talking about the evaluations given to you by SpaBat, for instance, but your assessment, what was it based on?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends on what you called "serious indications".

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I don't have time to expound. I would very much like to but I don't have enough time. Just to deal with this matter, I would need a whole lot more time because I consider it to be very significant in your assessments thereof: But I'm asking you what guided to you to say of Mr. Bagaric, who as you said was at the head of an organisation that behaved decently and honourably - I agree with that because there weren't many examples in the war in Bosnia of acts like this and you're probably aware of that, on the basis of reports from you're mission coming in - so why have you called him a nationalist what guided you, prompted you to call him a nationalist? Whether perhaps he had a pistol or he had a very strong temperament, I know him, yes, he was temperamental. So what led to you conclude that he was a nationalist and that is indeed what you did conclude?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Performance and statements.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Bravo, bravo, excellent. Did he make nationalistic statements, then? Did he make a single nationalistic statement that you can remember? You didn't mention any in your statement but I'm asking you now, can you remember any one?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not everything is in the reports, that's correct, but I don't think that I -- that I remember

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that I remember that after 14 years, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. I'm quite sure that had something been as significant, because you describe things in detail, you would have described this one too, had you heard something like that. Now I'd like to move on to another area and for that I need to look at P 03369. It's your report, where you speak about the hawks and doves but we are not going to deal with that now. P 03369 is the document number I'd like us to look at. Just tell me when you've found it, will you?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have it, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'll focus on point 6 where you have other points, number 6 is "Other points", and you said we visited SpaBat yesterday and we got the following information. "Mr. Boban said", and the Prosecutor showed you this document, but skipped over this part, "Mr. Boban said that UNPROFOR UNMOs and ECMM will not be able to enter Mostar for at least one month." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember it but it's in the report so it was noticed by us.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did you believe, sir, that the information you received from SpaBat was correct? Because this is SpaBat information, did you believe it?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably they had reason or -- I can't recall how this came to us, by SpaBat of course, but it could be that the commander visited Mr. Boban or the other way around. I don't know. But this was serious information by the Spanish Battalion so we considered this as a serious information.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes. I think it is indeed serious information but up until then you said that on several occasions you tried to enter Mostar but -- and you sought permission in different quarters but you weren't able to obtain this and I'm talking about the 10th of July. Now this piece of information where by Mr. Boban said that you wouldn't be able to enter Mostar, did you happen to inform anybody of that? And let me remind you yesterday you were shown a document - we don't have to look at it now, I'm sure you'll remember it - of the 2nd of August 1993, it is P -- for the transcript P 03900. It is the discussion with Mr. Prlic and the document was signed by Mr. Martin Garrod, and he arrived sometime after Mr. Nissen; isn't that right, that is to say after the 24th of July, that's when he reached Mostar. Did you inform him about this, that you had information whereby Mr. Boban, in actual fact, had prohibited or said that the observers wouldn't be able to enter Mostar for at least a month? Did you inform him of that?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This information, as I explained earlier, was shared by the heads of the coordination centre so they were aware of this remark.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Correct. And for the record, I'll say that it is document 2D 0 -- no, I beg your pardon, P 03362, P 03362 is the document number. It's the first document in the binder. And it's the same report, is it not, where we have on that first page - and in Croatian, it is the second page - where this was conveyed at least according to the SpaBat representatives, Boban said that UNPROFOR, the UNMOs, and the ECMM will not be able to enter Mostar for at least another month. Now the M2 team, et cetera. Do you remember whether you or somebody from your team, a colleague of yours or perhaps somebody else, tried to reach Mr. Boban to ask permission from him or at least an explanation as to why one couldn't enter Mostar?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You don't know, right. Now I'm going to ask you this. On the 22nd of August, as far as I remember, you were still on the territory of Herzegovina, am I right?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 22nd, you said?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: 22nd of August? Preparing for my leave. I think I left on the 23rd, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'd ask you then to look at P 04430. It's the second document in my binder. And it is dated the 22nd. They are military observers, they wrote this on the 22nd of August. It is page 6 of the English and look at F4, please. F4. When you've found it, let me know.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I found it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Right. It says, "Restrictions of movement". The HVO still denies access to Mostar. It is assumed that Mr. Boban has to be back from Geneva to reverse the order and let the UNMOs in. So this in a way confirms the information you received from SpaBat, does it not, that it was Mr. Boban's decision, right? I'm asking you -- now, tell me sir, do you happen to know that the observers from your organisation were the first, pursuant to Mr. Boban's authorisation -- we didn't have the answer in the transcript. Your answer was yes, I believe.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And to round off this topic, do you know, sir, that the observers of your mission were the first to enter Mostar with approval from Mr. Boban on the 24th, two days after you left the mission, the 24th of August 1993, and the humanitarian convoy entered the next day? Did you know this?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because I left.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did you know who Mr. Boban was, what place he held in the political and military structure?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you tell me or rather can you tell Their Honours what you know about this?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the president of HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Do you know that in the military structure he was the Supreme Commander of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Now we'll briefly move to the topic of prisons. I'll ask you to look at Prosecution Exhibit P 02721. Today, there has been a lot said about this but I will refer only to the part that refers to Mr. Stojic. P 02721. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is it --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: It's the Prosecution's exhibit.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: This is your report dated the 11th of June 1993, and I'm referring to point 3, "Other topics", and let me just remind you of the following. You say that when you visited the Heliodrom, that the deputy warden met you. There are 60 to 70 HVO soldiers, criminals, there. I don't know whether he told you that or whether you wrote it down. Eight civilians from other prisons, 11 Serbs and 431 prisoners from the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that there are about 10 women. This breakdown of prisoners, did the deputy warden give you this when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. That is what we noted from his mouth.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: As you responded to my colleague, you did not note down the names of any of the prisoners you spoke to or what they told you.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Would you please now look at P 02806? 2806.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, I'm referring to point 5 and I'll tell you right away that this is a conversation with Mr. Stojic, the document is dated the 16th of June 1993, and you discussed various topics with him. My colleague Peter Murphy will ask you about some of these but I'm interested in the prisoners now and here you say Mr. Stojic stated that the 504 prisoners in the Heliodrom are until now still not accused but under investigation. Did you ask Mr. Stojic about these 504 prisoners or did he supply this number? Did you suggest the number to him? I'm asking you this because you visited the prison on the 11th of June, whereas you talked to him on the 16th. So even if Mr. Stojic was sitting in the prison, the number would not be the same. Did you tell him, well, we visited the Heliodrom and that's the number that's there? Was that what happened?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall where the 504 comes from, but when it is in this report, then we noted that number, and he mentioned that number probably, because it doesn't come from us.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Sir, I'm showing you these documents so that we can draw some logical conclusions. I first showed you P 02721, where you visited the prison, and then you said the deputy director said that in the prison, there were 504 prisoners. I'm asking you now did Mr. Stojic tell you there were 504 or was it you who asked him what about those 504 prisoners because it's not logical to conclude that there would be exactly the same number on the 16th as on the 11th, because in prisons people come and go.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. Well, as you don't remember, it's probably futile to ask you this, but did you ask Mr. Stojic about the breakdown, the structure of the prisoners, as the deputy director described it to you? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Sir, there was mention about investigations being carried out but no indictments being brought. Look at D 200505 [as interpreted], please. It's in my pink binder, the second document from the top. 2D -- 2D 00505. The second from the bottom in my binder.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: We'll be very brief because my time is running out. It's a letter from the 3rd Battalion of the Military Police of the Department for Crime Prevention. And the one report is from the 9th of July 1993, to the police -- military police administration and it says that 313 criminal reports were submitted against members of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and it explains why these reports were submitted and then in the last passage, you say that -- it says that in the course of today, investigations or rather they will be processed and criminal reports will be submitted against 32 of them. Sir, I know you're not familiar with this document, but can you confirm that it's quite logical that in a structure such as the HVO, certain services did their job and Mr. Stojic would have provided information based on the information he received from them? Would you be able to say something about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, I'm going to object to that question on the basis of this document because it doesn't indicate, I don't believe, that any of the prisoners that we have been talking about here, Heliodrom prisoners, are prisoners being referred to in this document. This document relates to some people who were in detention in Ljubuski, and it discusses a number of criminal complaints, but it doesn't link in any way, as far as I can see, to any of the people who are at the Heliodrom at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I had noticed that. Ms. Nozica, this document does not directly deal with Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours. On the second page, it says that 600 persons expelled from Ljubuski, from Croatia there but the witness did not note down names of persons. Had the witness noted down the names of persons he spoke to, it would have been relatively easy for us to establish whether criminal reports were filed against these people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please ask the question. He doesn't know the document but please ask the question now.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to show the witness one more document and then I'll ask a question about both. 00506, 2D 00506, the last document in my binder. Last one that's bound.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And please tell me when you have found it.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: This is a report from the district military prosecutions office, prosecutor's office, in Mostar dated the 9th of July 1993 about the first semester that you discussed with Mr. Stojic. And in this report, it says that in this period, the prosecutor's office received 241 criminal reports against 1.674 individuals. I know that you are not familiar with this document, but I will tell you that in this entire period, 76 persons were indicted, or rather, indictments -- that number of indictments were brought against another number of persons. Are you aware that the judicial organs and the police organs were doing their job at that time? Did you have any contact with the judiciary? Did you know that the judicial organs were carrying out their job in relation to any person in detention?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I offer the same objection. There is no connection. The original point is whether there is an investigation or indictment of people who were being held at the Heliodrom, and again there is no connection between that and then what's referred to in this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Ms. Nozica?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Your Honours, I was not trying to establish a link, but my -- the two questions are linked much more than the documents shown by the Prosecutor mentioning "balija" or "balije". The Prosecutor showed a completely -- a document completely unfamiliar to the witness. My question was whether the witness had any contacts with the judiciary and whether he knew that there were judicial organs doing their work, doing their job in the HZ HB. That was my question. Nothing more.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, please take a look at another document of yours, P 03007.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. Before we move to this exhibit, there is one thing I'd like to note about this document coming from the military prosecutor. On paragraph 2, it says that the military police for the HVO submitted 1.394 criminal complaints, MUP submitted 267 of these complaints, and the military police of the ABiH would have sent four criminal complaints. Therefore, it seems that the ABiH directly sent to the military prosecutor a number of criminal complaints. This is something I would like to state. Thank you. You can resume.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
